title: Who Knocked?
briefing: Ticket SEC-2231: the monitoring bot says web1 had an out-of-hours login from an address nobody recognises. Sit down at the SOC desk and read the logs on web1 and db1 (or open a console on a server and use ls, cat, grep and tail). Then file the incident report: which IP address the attacker used, what kind of attack it was, and which account they got into. You only get a few wrong answers per field, so find the evidence first.

objectives.description: Report the account the attacker got into

debrief: The attacker at 203.0.113.45 tried dozens of passwords against root, admin and other common names within a few minutes, then got into the deploy account: that burst of failures followed by an accepted login is the signature of an SSH brute-force attack. Other addresses in the logs look suspicious but are not the answer: one scanner only failed a handful of times and never got in, and the deploy account also logs in legitimately by key from the CI server. A real admin would count failures per address (grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log, then sort and count by source), check who is logged in with who and last, lock or reset the deploy account, and read what the attacker did through sudo. To prevent it: disable password logins for SSH and use keys, deny root logins, and add rate limiting or fail2ban.
